clue.text: Secretary caught providing information about peacemaking

parts.note: a PA is a personal assistant, the secretary of an office
c = caught, the mark a cricket scorecard puts against a batter
'providing' introduces a condition, and so does 'if'
i is the sign for information, on tourist boards and help desks
c = circa, the 'about' that goes before an uncertain date

explanation.surface: An office secretary is caught passing on what she knows about the peace talks.
explanation.walkthrough: C turns up twice for two different reasons — cricket's 'caught' and circa's 'about' — which is a fair warning that one letter can have several owners. Five pieces in a row is a lot for a short answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pacific means peace-making or peace-loving; the ocean was named for that sense rather than lending it.

clue.text: Knock biting lice off bird

indicators.note: biting means taking between the jaws, so the word for knock goes around the other letters

parts.note: to knock something is to criticise it, to pan it

indicators.note: off in the sense of gone bad or out of order, so the letters of lice are rearranged

explanation.surface: Instructions for getting rid of lice that are chewing on a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges LICE into ELIC, and 'biting' puts PAN (knock, criticise) round it.
explanation.definitionFit: The pelican is a large water bird with a big throat pouch for scooping fish.

clue.text: Churches hosting geriatric centre with a tea dance …

indicators.note: a host keeps guests inside the house, so whatever is hosted goes within
the centre of a word is the single letter standing equidistant from both ends

parts.note: ch = church, written twice over for the plural
the middle letter of the nine in geriAtric
the clue's own 'a', taken at face value
cha is British slang for tea, from the same Chinese word as 'char'

explanation.surface: A church hall is laying on a tea dance for the local old folk.
explanation.walkthrough: The same three letters arrive three times by three different routes, and only the last of them is the tea. 'Geriatric centre' reads as a day centre and means one letter out of the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: The cha-cha-cha is a Cuban ballroom dance, named after the shuffle of quick steps its rhythm calls for.

clue.text: … in hall some Surrey officials set up

indicators.note: 'some' asks for a part of what follows rather than the whole of it
in a down clue what is set up runs the other way, read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: SurREY OFficials holds REYOF, which a down entry reads upwards

explanation.surface: Some of Surrey's officials are setting themselves up in a hall.
explanation.walkthrough: Hidden answers live on the join between two words, which is why 'Surrey officials' has to be read as one run of letters and not as two things. Down entries are where a reversal can be called setting up.
explanation.definitionFit: A foyer is the hall you walk into at a theatre or a hotel — the entrance space, not a passage.

clue.text: Historical record or cliche circulated about north?

indicators.note: something circulated about has been passed from hand to hand, and it does not come back in the order it went out

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
n = north on the compass

explanation.surface: A tired old cliche is doing the rounds up north.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that 'north' is in the clue for its initial alone. Eight letters of fodder plus one abbreviation is the standard build of a long anagram, so count before you look for anything cleverer.
explanation.definitionFit: A chronicle sets events down in the order they happened, which is what makes it a historical record rather than a history.

clue.text: More fragile West Indies arachnid died out

indicators.note: something put out has been taken away from where it was sitting

parts.note: WI is the West Indies, as it appears on a cricket scoreboard
an arachnid is a SPIDER, and the D goes
d = died, the letter a family tree uses, and it is the one removed

explanation.surface: A spider from the West Indies has died out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Died out' carries the whole deletion and reads as plain extinction, which is why nothing in the surface looks like an instruction. The comparative in 'More fragile' tells you the answer ends in -ER before you have a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A wisp is a thin frail strand of hair or smoke, so wispier is more fragile — the comparative the clue asks for outright.

clue.text: Weathers storms when woman put out rubbish

indicators.note: a word that storms will not stay where it is put, and neither will its letters
to put something out is to shift it off the premises, so those letters leave

parts.note: WEATHERS with the woman's three letters gone leaves five to rearrange
'her' stands in for the woman, and this is what is put out

explanation.surface: He weathers whatever storms come while a woman puts the rubbish out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weathers storms' is the one stretch of the clue that reads as plain English, and both words are machinery. The deletion has to happen before the shuffle, which is the order the clue itself gives.
explanation.definitionFit: Waste is rubbish in the municipal sense — household waste, what goes in the bin rather than what is said in an argument.

clue.text: Hunkering down occupying building

definitions.meaning: the physical sense: crouched on your heels
the legal sense: living in an empty property without the owner's leave

explanation.surface: Someone is crouched down inside a building they have taken over.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are the same word, so there is nothing to assemble and nothing to remove; the only question is which two senses the setter wants. British law has a particular name for the second, which is why 'occupying building' reads as legal shorthand.
explanation.definitionFit: Squatting is crouching on your heels, and it is also living in a building you have no right to — one verb, two unrelated acts.

clue.text: Repository for television at home

parts.note: someone at home is in
the box is what British households have called the television since it was furniture

explanation.surface: A cabinet at home to keep the television in.
explanation.walkthrough: The two pieces come in the opposite order to the clue, so build from the definition rather than reading left to right. 'Repository' is deliberately grand for something that mostly holds unread email.
explanation.definitionFit: An inbox is where post is put and left until it is dealt with, on a desk or on a screen — a repository in the plainest sense.

clue.text: Discounted wine clubs as part of university education

parts.note: red is wine

indicators.note: as part of means the clubs letter is placed within the following letters

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs, the card suit

explanation.surface: Cheap wine for societies, all part of a student's university life.
explanation.definitionFit: Reduced means lowered in price, sold at a discount.

clue.text: On choppy lake, back of dinghy losing water

indicators.note: on here places one piece beside the other, the end of the dinghy coming after the lake
choppy water is rough and broken, so the letters of lake are tossed into a new order
the back of a word is its last letter, here of dinghy

parts.note: the last letter of dinghy is Y

explanation.surface: A small boat on a rough lake is shipping water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'choppy' rearranges LAKE into LEAK, and 'back of' gives Y, the last letter of dinghy, set 'On' it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something leaky lets liquid seep out through holes or cracks, so it is losing water.

clue.text: Attempt to save doubtful bride succeeded with signal received

indicators.note: a doubtful account is one you cannot rely on, and these letters cannot be relied on to stay in place
what is received is taken in, so it goes inside

parts.note: five of the six letters that get rearranged
s = succeeded, the letter used of one monarch following another
a cue is the signal an actor waits for

explanation.surface: The attempt to save a hesitant bride came off once the signal was received.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge a rescue bid pulls your partner out of a contract that is heading down. Only six letters are being shuffled; the middle three are handed to you intact and simply dropped in.
explanation.definitionFit: A rescue bid is bridge's name for a bid made to save a partner from a hopeless contract, and it has spread to any last-ditch effort to save something.

clue.text: At this point dividing care of new church makes sense

indicators.note: what divides something comes down in the middle of it and splits it in two

parts.note: c/o on an envelope = care of
n = new, as on a product label
CE is the Church of England
at this point = here

explanation.surface: Splitting the running of a new church between people is the sensible move now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At this point' is scene-setting in the surface and the longest single piece of the answer, which is the kind of swap worth looking for first. C/O comes off an envelope and CE is the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Coherence is the quality of parts that hang together, which is what we mean when we say an argument makes sense.

clue.text: Endless exotica could be harmful

indicators.note: a word with no ends has lost the letter standing at each end of it
'could be' says these letters could make something else, which is licence to reorder them

parts.note: EXOTICA with the letter at each end taken off

explanation.surface: Exotic goods without end could do you damage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' strips both ends here, not just the last letter, and the arithmetic says so: exotica has seven letters and the answer has five. The count is what settles which reading of an indicator was meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Toxic means poisonous, and poison is harmful by definition; the word now stretches to anything damaging, from waste to workplaces.

clue.text: Speciality of hotel in French resort

indicators.note: 'in' puts what comes before it inside what comes after

parts.note: Nice is the resort city on the French Riviera
h = hotel in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: The speciality of a hotel somewhere on the French coast.
explanation.walkthrough: Hotel is H from the radio alphabet, which setters raid constantly — alpha, bravo, charlie, delta, echo, hotel, india, victor. Once you see that, only one five-letter resort will take a letter in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A niche is the speciality a business or a creature has carved out — the corner of the market that is nobody else's.

clue.text: First lady's online, endlessly long annually

parts.note: Eve, the first woman, is on line, read as EVE placed on RY, the abbreviation for railway line

indicators.note: endlessly means the last letter of the word for long is cut off

parts.note: to long for something is to yearn for it

explanation.surface: A president's wife is always on the internet and wants to be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'online' is read as 'on line': EVE (the first lady in Genesis) is on RY (railway line). 'endlessly' trims YEARN to YEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done every year happens once each twelve months, which is what annually means.

clue.text: So excited to be out and about at the same time

definitions.note: 'About' here means around or in existence, so the phrase describes things present together; the answer supplies the past tense that the phrase itself leaves open.

indicators.note: letters that are out are no longer in their places and have to be put back some other way

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters — exactly the length wanted

explanation.surface: Two people are delighted to be out and about together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Excited' is a stock anagram instruction, which is exactly why it is fodder here; the instruction is 'to be out'. Count the letters of the first two words against the enumeration and the clue gives itself away.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that coexisted were about — around, in existence — over one and the same stretch of time, which is all the word claims.

clue.text: Join Tina Turner to put on a show?

parts.note: to join a club or the army is to enter it

indicators.note: a turner is something that turns, so it signals the letters of Tina being turned around into a new order

explanation.surface: An invitation to team up with the singer Tina Turner for a performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turner' looks like part of the singer's name, but it is the anagram signal: TINA becomes TAIN after ENTER.
explanation.definitionFit: To entertain an audience is to amuse them with a performance, like putting on a show; the question mark flags the loose fit.

clue.text: Three assembled by river to make den

indicators.note: by means next to, so the river comes beside the reordered letters
assembled means put together in a new arrangement, so the letters of three are reordered

parts.note: the Ouse is a river in England, flowing through York

explanation.surface: Three people gather beside a river to build a hideout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'assembled' rearranges THREE into TREEH, then OUSE, the English river, comes 'by' it.
explanation.definitionFit: A treehouse is a children's hideaway built among branches, a private den.

clue.text: Final word describing complex model causes perplexity

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw it round something, so what describes goes on the outside

parts.note: amen is the final word of a prayer
t = model, from Ford's Model T
a maze is a complex of paths; 'complex' is the noun here

explanation.surface: A final word about a complicated model leaves everybody baffled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Describing' is the container instruction in its geometrical sense — a circle described about a square goes round the outside of it. Ford's Model T is one of the most dependable single letters in the crossword.
explanation.definitionFit: Amazement and perplexity are both the state of being thrown by something you cannot account for.

clue.text: Good-natured sailor supporting fellows hampered by beer

indicators.note: what supports a thing stands underneath it, and in a down entry underneath means further along

parts.note: ale is beer, and it opens up to take the others in

indicators.note: to be hampered by something is to be caught up inside it

parts.note: f = fellow, doubled to make it plural
AB is an able seaman

explanation.surface: A sailor is backing up his fellows, all of them slowed down by beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporting' only means 'below' because this is a down entry; in an across clue it would have nothing to say. Doubling a letter for a plural — FF for fellows — is standard, like pp for pages.
explanation.definitionFit: An affable person is easy and pleasant to fall into talk with, which is good-natured in its everyday sense.

clue.text: Ogre edgily suppresses craving for food

indicators.note: to suppress something is to hold it down out of sight, which is where these letters are

parts.note: oGRE EDgily — the letters run straight on across the gap

explanation.surface: A nervous ogre is keeping his appetite in check.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edgily' is in the clue to lend two letters, not to describe anyone, and the join between the words is exactly where hidden answers sit. An ogre with an appetite is the sort of picture that keeps you hunting for a charade.
explanation.definitionFit: Greed for food is the appetite that will not stop when it has had enough, which is why it made the list of deadly sins.

clue.text: Down payment for silicon in warehouse

indicators.note: 'in' places what comes before it inside what comes after

parts.note: a depot is a warehouse or store
Si is silicon's symbol in the periodic table

explanation.surface: A down payment on a consignment of silicon held at the warehouse.
explanation.walkthrough: Chemical symbols are worth learning as a set — Si, Fe, Sn, Pb — because they hand a setter two letters wrapped in an ordinary word. Here the silicon is real enough in the surface to pass unexamined.
explanation.definitionFit: A deposit is the part of the price you put down to hold a purchase, on a car or a flat — the down payment itself.

clue.text: Boat's gear regularly surrounded by small fish

indicators.note: take the letters at regular intervals — every second one — rather than all of them

parts.note: fry are small fish, the newly hatched ones

indicators.note: what surrounds a thing closes on it from both sides

parts.note: every second letter of gEaR

explanation.surface: A boat's tackle keeps getting hemmed in by little fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' takes every other letter, and which of the two sets you want is settled by what fits — here the second and the fourth. Fry are small fish, which is where the phrase 'small fry' comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: A ferry is a boat that works a fixed crossing rather than going wherever it likes.

clue.text: Provokes teacher to retire over student with low grade

indicators.note: over here means covering, so the reversed teacher sits around the next letters
to retire is to go back, so the word for teacher is read backwards

parts.note: pupils address a male teacher as sir
L is for learner, the student driver's plate
E is a low grade in exams

explanation.surface: A teacher is driven to quit after marking a weak student.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to retire' reverses SIR to RIS, and 'over' wraps it round L (learner) and E (a poor grade).
explanation.definitionFit: To rile someone is to annoy or irritate them, which is to provoke them.

clue.text: Crumple cups scattered around empty coach after race

indicators.note: around means the jumbled letters enclose the rest
scattered means strewn about, so the letters of cups are put in a jumbled order
after means the letters from coach follow the word for race

parts.note: to race is to run

indicators.note: empty means the inside of coach is removed, keeping its first and last letters

parts.note: coach with its inner letters removed leaves its first and last letters, C and H

explanation.surface: Someone crumples paper cups and throws them around a deserted coach after a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scattered' gives SCUP from CUPS, split as SC...UP 'around' RUN (race) and CH, which is coach made 'empty'.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrunch up paper is to crush it into a ball, which is crumpling it.

clue.text: Watched very good journalist following lead for story

indicators.note: following means the other pieces come after the first letter
the lead for a word is its first letter, here of story

parts.note: the first letter of story is S
PI is short for pious, very good
ED is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A worthy reporter keeps an eye on a tip that might become a news story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lead for' gives S, the first letter of story, with PI (pious) and ED (editor) 'following' it.
explanation.definitionFit: To have spied something is to have observed it, often secretly, so to have watched it.

clue.text: Inside Shogun in Japan there's a warrior

indicators.note: 'inside' says the letters are being held within the words rather than made out of them

parts.note: shoguN IN JApan — the letters run on across both gaps

explanation.surface: Somewhere inside the Shogun's Japan there is a warrior.
explanation.walkthrough: A shogun was Japan's military ruler, which is what lets the surface hold together while the letters quietly cross two word boundaries. Long hiding places are easier to find than short ones once you start looking.
explanation.definitionFit: A ninja was a covert agent and mercenary of feudal Japan, trained to fight — a warrior, though one who worked in the dark.

clue.text: Everyone tucked into Ribena supply for dancer

indicators.note: tucked into means placed inside the other letters
supply read as supple-ly, flexibly, so the letters of Ribena are bent into a new order

parts.note: everyone means all

explanation.surface: A dancer's whole troupe gets stuck into a stock of the blackcurrant cordial Ribena.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supply' is read as 'supplely': RIBENA bends into BERINA, split as B...ERINA, with ALL 'tucked into' it. Ribena is a British blackcurrant drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballerina is a female ballet dancer, especially one in a leading role.

clue.text: Naming words for numbers including one in French

indicators.note: what is included sits inside the thing that includes it

parts.note: nos. is the plural of no., the abbreviation for number
un is French for one

explanation.surface: The words that name the numbers, one of them French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One in French' reads as though 'in' were the instruction; the instruction is 'including', and the French is only supplying UN. Nos. for numbers comes straight off an invoice.
explanation.definitionFit: Nouns are the naming words of grammar — the class that gives a thing its name, taught under exactly that phrase in primary school.

clue.text: Made certain rocky undersea area's ignored

indicators.note: a rocky road is uneven and unsettled, and so are these letters
what is ignored is left out of account altogether

parts.note: UNDERSEA without its A, leaving seven letters to rearrange
a = area, and this is the letter ignored

explanation.surface: A rocky patch of seabed is being left out of the survey.
explanation.walkthrough: The A has to come out before the rearranging, because seven letters are wanted and 'undersea' offers eight. 'Area's ignored' is a whole deletion instruction that reads as scenery.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensure an outcome is to see to it that it cannot fail, which is making certain of it.

clue.text: Most stingy relatives?

definitions.meaning: near in its old sense of mean with money
the family sense, leaning on the set phrase that ends 'and dearest'

explanation.surface: A question about whether your relatives are the tightest-fisted people you know.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark warns that the second half is not a straight synonym: it leans on the set phrase 'nearest and dearest'. 'Near' for miserly is old-fashioned British, and still current enough to clue with.
explanation.definitionFit: Near is an old British word for mean with money, so the nearest are the stingiest; and your nearest are your close family.
